title: Local Euclidean spaces
body:
A manifold lets us do calculus on a space without first flattening the whole space into one Euclidean map. A local description gives enough coordinates to differentiate functions and describe motion. Smooth conversions on overlaps make those calculations compatible.
On the soil scientists' two-dimensional terrain, the points are actual ground locations. A flat board supplies nearby labels; it does not assert that lengths on the board equal lengths on the ground. Temperature values and routes belong to the surface, whichever scientist records them.
General relativity uses a four-dimensional spacetime manifold. A metric is added to say what clocks and rulers measure. Local coordinate structure alone neither supplies that measurement nor declares the space flat.
statement: Local coordinates allow calculus without assuming a globally flat space.

title: Compatible local coordinate descriptions
statement: A smooth \(n\)-manifold has compatible local \(n\)-coordinate descriptions; a metric is extra structure.

title: Terrain survey: one surface
body:
Let \(M\) be the ground surface of a kame-and-kettle landscape. Scientists use overlapping patches, each labelled by projecting ground points smoothly onto a rigid board's grid. A patch is small enough that the projection has a smooth inverse; two numbers locate a ground point.
Temperature \(T(p)\) and a measured curvature estimate \(K(p)\) assign scalar readings to points \(p\). Surface grass growth assigns a tangent direction and magnitude instead. Two scientists can record different coordinates for the same peg while agreeing on its temperature.
The boards can have different scales, orientations and oblique axes. Their overlap rules let the group reconcile the records into one surface description. The manifold is this collection of points with its compatible local structure, not the collection of physical boards.
\explanation{dimension}{Why is this still two-dimensional?}{A location needs two independent local labels. Height in an embedding picture is constrained by the surface and is not a third direction in which one can move while staying on it. Curvature changes geometry, not this local dimension.}
statement: Overlapping grids describe one two-dimensional ground surface, not separate flat pieces.

title: Coordinates as labels
body:
A coordinate chart assigns numbers to points in some local region of a manifold. The numbers are labels rather than physical structure: changing the chart changes the component description without changing the underlying point.
A point \(p\) is an element of the manifold; \(x(p)\) is the tuple one chart gives it. The inverse map \(x^{-1}\) is essential because a calculation with labels must still identify a unique point.
For the terrain survey, projection onto a straight board grid defines one such labelling over a sufficiently small patch. Axes need not be orthogonal and their scale need not measure ground distance. That freedom is why a metric is separate from a coordinate chart.
statement: Coordinates label points; they do not prescribe lengths or angles.

title: An invertible local labelling
statement: A chart \(x:U\to x(U)\subset\mathbb R^n\) gives a smooth, invertible local labelling.

title: Terrain survey: one board
body:
Each scientist works on a small region \(U\) and uses a straight grid on a rigid tangent board to define \(x:U\rightarrow\mathbb R^2\). Ground points are mapped smoothly and one-to-one onto the board, whose axes may be differently scaled and need not be perpendicular. The patch must be small enough that the projection and its inverse remain smooth and unambiguous.
Those two coordinate numbers let the scientist write temperature as a function and record the probe's track as \(x^1(t),x^2(t)\). They label the curved ground; they do not replace it with a flat surface. The board is tangent at its reference point, not at every point of the patch. Coordinate basis vectors elsewhere follow the surface coordinate curves there, rather than the fixed arrows drawn on the board.
\explanation{overlap}{Why do different boards still describe one motion?}{On an overlap the scientists agree a smooth conversion \(y^i=y^i(x^1,x^2)\). Substituting the same track \(x^j(t)\) gives its new description \(y^i(t)\). The chain rule relates its coordinate rates:
\[\frac{dy^i}{dt}=\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}\frac{dx^j}{dt}.\]
Here \(j=1,2\) is summed. The numbers change; no ground point or physical route moves merely because its labels change.}
statement: A board projection supplies local labels while the measured ground stays curved.

title: Changing labels, not points
body:
A coordinate transformation changes the numerical labels assigned to manifold points while leaving the points themselves unchanged. In GR this freedom is larger than the Lorentz transformations of SR: curved spacetime generally needs arbitrary smooth changes between local coordinate charts.
If a peg has labels \(x(p)\) and \(y(p)\), the transition identifies those two numerical records. It does not send the peg to a new physical location.
A scalar's value stays the same, but its formula in the labels usually changes. A vector's components change too, because the coordinate basis changes. Distinguishing the object from its coordinate description is the point of the transition machinery.
statement: A change of coordinates alters descriptions, not the underlying points or measurements.

title: The overlap transition
body:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be overlapping \cref{charts}{math.coordinate_chart}. For a point \(p\) in their common region, the transition map takes \(x(p)\) to \(y(p)\). It is a smooth map between open subsets of coordinate space, with a smooth inverse.
The notation \(y^i=y^i(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\) abbreviates this composition; the inverse gives \(x^i=x^i(y)\). A relabelling moves no physical point and changes no measured scalar value.
\explanation{scalar}{Does the temperature formula stay the same?}{The reading stays the same, but its formula usually changes. Write \(T_x=T\circ x^{-1}\) and \(T_y=T\circ y^{-1}\). Then
\[T_y(y(p))=T(p)=T_x(x(p)).\]
For example, replacing a metre label by a centimetre label changes the numerical argument of the formula. This is why an invariant measurement need not have an unchanged coordinate expression.}
statement: The transition \(y\circ x^{-1}\) converts labels for the same point on an overlap.

title: Terrain survey: reconciling neighbours
statement: Straight board grids can give nonlinear transitions when they project different curved patches.

title: Jacobian of the change
body:
For overlapping charts \(x\) and \(y\), write the transition as \(y=y(x)\). The derivatives \(J^i{}_j=\partial y^i/\partial x^j\) form its Jacobian. At each overlap point it is invertible. A nonlinear transition can have a Jacobian that varies with position.
For a smooth probe route, the chain rule gives
\[\frac{dy^i}{dt}=J^i{}_j\frac{dx^j}{dt}.\]
Repeated \(j\) is summed over the coordinate directions. The components change; the probe's motion does not.
\explanation{inverse}{Why is the Jacobian invertible?}{Differentiate the inverse transition and compose the two chain rules:
\[\frac{\partial x^k}{\partial y^i}\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}=\delta^k{}_j.\]
The derivative matrices are inverses. A zero determinant would signal a failure of these coordinates, not automatically a physical singularity.}
Later tensor component rules use these same Jacobian and inverse-Jacobian factors.
statement: The Jacobian converts infinitesimal coordinate changes; its inverse reverses the conversion.

title: Lorentz transformations as a special case
body: The \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} are special coordinate transformations between inertial frames in flat spacetime. General coordinate transformations need not be linear, global, or tied to inertial observers.
statement: Lorentz transformations are a restricted class of spacetime coordinate changes.

title: Not a change of physics
body: Changing coordinates is not the same as changing the physical situation. A badly chosen coordinate system can make simple geometry look complicated, and a well chosen one can simplify a calculation, but neither changes the manifold point or the coordinate-independent statement being described.
statement: Relabelling a physical situation does not change it.

title: A history through spacetime
body: A worldline is the curve traced by a particle, observer, clock, detector, or light signal through spacetime. It turns a sequence of \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event} into one geometric object.
statement: A worldline records a history through spacetime, not just a spatial track.

title: A parametrised spacetime history
body:
A smooth worldline is a map \(\gamma:I\to M\) from a real parameter interval \(I\) into a spacetime \cref{manifold}{math.manifold} \(M\). In a chart its coordinate functions are \(x^\mu(\lambda)\). The parameter \(\lambda\) labels successive events along the history of a particle or signal. For a massive clock it is often convenient to use \cref{Proper time}{sr.proper_time} \(\tau\); a light ray has no proper-time clock parameter of this kind.
\explanation{parameter}{Is the parameter another spacetime coordinate?}{No. It labels positions along this particular curve. The spacetime point \(\gamma(\lambda)\) already has its coordinate tuple. Two smooth monotonic parameter choices can describe the same oriented path while assigning different rates to its traversal. Physical time or proper time, when supplied, gives the rate a particular meaning.}
statement: A worldline is a curve \(\gamma:I\to M\) through spacetime, labelled by a parameter.

title: Curve versus coordinate plot
body:
A curve \(\gamma\) specifies points of the manifold. A \cref{chart}{math.coordinate_chart} displays them as the coordinate functions \(x\circ\gamma\). Another chart gives \(y\circ\gamma\), usually with a different-looking graph.
A \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} is one useful spacetime display; the drawing is not the worldline itself. Merely choosing a more complicated coordinate plot does not make a freely moving particle accelerate physically.
statement: Different coordinate plots can represent exactly the same curve.

title: Terrain survey: the mobile probe
body:
The mobile probe follows a smooth route \(\gamma:t\mapsto\gamma(t)\in M\), with \(t\) in seconds. In one board chart its track is \((x^1(t),x^2(t))\). Across an overlap another scientist records \((y^1(t),y^2(t))\). The formulas change, but the route does not jump.
\explanation{history}{Is the surface route itself a worldline?}{Strictly this is a curve on the spatial terrain. Including time produces the spacetime history \(t\mapsto(t,\gamma(t))\). A stationary probe has a constant surface position but still traces a history through time. The distinction keeps a two-dimensional ground map separate from spacetime.}
statement: A surface route becomes a spacetime history when time is included.

title: Tangent direction
body:
For a smooth spacetime curve \(\gamma(\lambda)\), choose a chart \(x^\mu\) near the event \(p=\gamma(\lambda_0)\). Its tangent has components
\[v^\mu=\left.\frac{dx^\mu(\lambda)}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda_0}.\]
Changing chart changes these components by the chain rule. Changing parameter changes their common scale. Neither operation turns the vector into a finite displacement between separated events.
This tangent belongs to the \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space} at \(p\). For a massive particle, choosing \cref{proper time}{sr.proper_time} as parameter gives the \cref{velocity four-vector}{sr.velocity_four_vector}. That choice needs a metric and is unavailable for a null clock path.
statement: A smooth worldline has a tangent at each event; its scale depends on the parameter.

title: Timelike and null cases
body:
Once a Lorentzian metric \(g\) is supplied, it classifies a curve using its nonzero tangent \(v\). With mostly-minus signature, \(g(v,v)>0\) is timelike and \(g(v,v)=0\) is null. Reversing the metric signature reverses the timelike sign but leaves the null condition unchanged.
Material particles and physical clocks follow timelike histories; light in vacuum follows null histories. Spacelike curves can occur in diagrams but do not describe material objects or signals. A smooth manifold or coordinate chart alone cannot make this classification.
statement: A metric distinguishes timelike material histories from null light paths.

title: Local tangent directions
body: The attached plane pictures the vector space \(T_pM\), not a claim that the terrain is flat. The board agrees with a tangent plane at its reference point only; other ground points have their own tangent spaces. The surrounding three-dimensional drawing helps visualisation but is not required by the mathematical definition.
statement: On a two-dimensional surface, \(T_pM\) is a two-dimensional space of local directions.

title: Possible directions at one point
body:
A curved manifold has no single global vector space in which every arrow naturally lives. Instead each point \(p\) has its own tangent space \(T_pM\): the vector space of possible instantaneous directions through that point. Velocities, directional derivatives, infinitesimal displacements, and tangents to \cref{Worldlines}{math.worldline} are all tangent vectors.
The word local is essential. Two routes through one point can have the same instantaneous motion and different later bends. The tangent vector retains the first-order motion and forgets those later differences.
At another point there is another tangent space. Neither a coordinate chart nor the existence of vectors at both points supplies a preferred comparison between them. A transport rule is additional structure.
statement: Instantaneous motion is a local vector, even when its full route curves.

title: Vectors based at one point
body: The tangent space \(T_pM\) at \(p\) is the vector space of tangent vectors based at that one point. It has the same dimension as the manifold near \(p\). Coordinates provide a basis \(\partial/\partial x^\mu|_p\), but the space and its vectors do not depend on which coordinates are chosen.
statement: The \(n\)-dimensional vector space \(T_pM\) contains tangent vectors based at one point \(p\).

title: From curves to tangent vectors
body:
Choose smooth curves \(\gamma\) through the same point \(p\), with \(\gamma(0)=p\). In a chart \(x^i\), compare their derivatives \(v^i=dx^i/dt|_0\). Identify two curves when these derivatives agree. The parameter scale is part of this comparison.
For a \cref{coordinate transition}{math.coordinate_transformation} \(y^a=y^a(x)\), the chain rule gives
\[\left.\frac{dy^a}{dt}\right|_0
 =\left.\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}\right|_p v^i.\]
The chart Jacobian is invertible, so agreement in one chart is equivalent to agreement in the other. These equivalence classes are tangent vectors.
Their components can be added and scaled. Since every chart change acts by the same linear Jacobian at \(p\), these operations define a coordinate-independent vector space \(T_pM\) of dimension \(n\).
\explanation{equivalence}{Which curves have the same tangent?}{Two curves can have equal first derivatives at \(p\) and different second derivatives. They then represent the same tangent vector but can bend apart immediately afterwards. Only their first-order motion at the crossing enters the equivalence class.}
statement: Curves with the same first-order motion at a point represent the same tangent vector.

title: Tangent vectors as directional derivatives
body:
A tangent vector can be understood by what it does to smooth scalar functions. Routes with the same first-order motion through \(p\) give the same instantaneous readout on every smooth scalar field, even if they bend differently later. The measurement therefore needs the tangent at the crossing, not the probe's whole future path.
The parameter fixes the vector's scale: if \(t\) counts seconds, \(v\) is a velocity and \(v[f]\) is a change per second. No unit length or metric has been assumed.
Let \(p=\gamma(0)\), \(v=\dot\gamma(0)\) and \(f\) be a smooth scalar field. Define
\[v[f]\coloneqq\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_0.\]
For local labels \(x^1,x^2\) on the two-dimensional terrain, the ordinary chain rule gives
\[\begin{aligned}
v[f]&=v^1\partial_1f+v^2\partial_2f,\\
v^i&=\frac{dx^i}{dt},\qquad i=1,2.
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(\partial_i\) means differentiation with respect to \(x^i\). The chart makes the readout calculable; relabelling does not change the underlying motion or scalar rate.
statement: A tangent vector assigns each smooth scalar its directional rate of change.

title: Walking on a curved surface
body: Imagine standing at a point on a sphere. Every possible instantaneous walking velocity lies in the flat plane tangent to the sphere there, even though longer paths curve over the surface. This embedded picture is only an aid: an abstract manifold still has a tangent space even when it is not pictured inside a larger flat space.
statement: A tangent plane describes instantaneous directions, not a flat replacement for the surface.

title: Terrain survey: growth and motion
body: The terrain is a two-dimensional manifold, so at every ground point \(p\) its tangent space \(T_pM\) is a two-dimensional vector space. The grass-growth direction \(G_p\) and the probe velocity \(\dot\gamma\) lie in that space. The board is a useful picture of the tangent plane at its own reference point. Elsewhere in the patch, however, the coordinate basis vectors are tangent to the surface coordinate curves at that ground point; they are not literally the same fixed arrows drawn on the board.
statement: Grass growth and probe velocity at one ground point belong to the same tangent space.

title: Velocity is local
body: At an event \(p\) on a particle's worldline, the curve's tangent gives its instantaneous spacetime velocity. A later event \(q\) has a different tangent space \(T_qM\). On a curved manifold the two velocity vectors cannot be directly subtracted until a connection or transport rule explains how to compare vectors at different points.
statement: Comparing vectors at different points requires a specified identification or transport rule.

title: Basis and components
body:
For a chart \(x^i\) on an \(n\)-manifold, write \(\partial_i|_p\coloneqq\partial/\partial x^i|_p\). This coordinate basis acts on smooth scalar functions by differentiation. A tangent vector has the expansion
\[v=v^i\partial_i|_p,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\]
with the repeated index summed.
Changing to labels \(y^a\) changes the basis by the inverse Jacobian:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\bigg|_p
 =\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\bigg|_p\partial_i|_p.\]
The vector components change by the forward Jacobian. Substituting both rules into \(v=v_y^a\partial/\partial y^a|_p\) cancels the inverse factors, leaving the same vector.
Thus a component tuple without its basis is not a complete description. On an oblique or differently scaled coordinate grid, the components are not automatically physical lengths along perpendicular unit axes.
statement: Components and basis vectors change oppositely so their combined tangent vector stays fixed.

title: Coordinate units and tangent components
body:
Keep the curve parameter fixed when comparing components. If the probe's parameter is time in seconds, then \(v^x=dx/dt\) is a coordinate rate. A rate reported as \(0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) on a metre-labelled grid is \(50\,\mathrm{cm/s}\) on the corresponding centimetre-labelled grid. The probe's motion has not changed.

Writing the numerical coordinate readings as \(x'=100x\), the chain rule gives \[v^{x'}=100v^x,\qquad \partial_{x'}=\frac1{100}\partial_x.\] These changes cancel in \(v=v^x\partial_x+v^y\partial_y\). The basis matters as much as the components. On the surveyors' arbitrarily scaled or oblique grids, a coordinate rate is not by itself a measured speed: a metric is needed to turn the whole tangent vector into a physical speed.
statement: Changing coordinate units changes velocity components, not the motion they describe.

title: Infinitesimal is not finite
body: A tangent vector describes first-order motion at one point; it is not automatically an arrow joining two separated manifold points. Turning a finite separation into a tangent vector requires extra choices, such as a coordinate construction or a geodesic map, and may not be unique.
statement: A tangent vector describes first-order motion at one point, not a finite separation.

title: Linear questions about directions
body: A \cref{tangent vector}{math.tangent_space} describes a possible instantaneous motion. A covector is a linear readout of such a vector. Why does physics need both? Follow a temperature probe across the soil scientists' curved two-dimensional terrain: its motion is a vector, while the temperature field supplies the readout.
statement: A covector is a linear readout of a tangent vector at one point.

title: A direction asks a temperature question
body:
The smooth, time-independent temperature field gives a reading \(T(p)\) at each ground point. Motion along an isotherm gives zero instantaneous temperature change; another direction can warm or cool the probe. Let its route be \(\gamma(t)\), with \(t\) in seconds, and its tangent velocity at \(p=\gamma(0)\) be \(v\).
A tangent vector acts on a smooth scalar by directional differentiation:
\[v[T]\coloneqq\left.\frac{d}{dt}T(\gamma(t))\right|_0.\]
This readout depends on the first-order motion at \(p\), not on the probe's later route.
The temperature differential is defined to give that readout:
\[dT_p(v)\coloneqq v[T].\]
At a fixed point this rule is linear in \(v\). A linear rule on \(T_pM\) is a covector, and all those rules form the cotangent space \(T_p^*M\).
\explanation{linearity}{Why is the readout linear?}{Tangent vectors act as directional-derivative operators. Their linear combinations act on a scalar field by
\[(a v+b w)[T]=a\,v[T]+b\,w[T].\]
Thus the definition gives
\[dT_p(a v+b w)=a\,dT_p(v)+b\,dT_p(w).\]
The numbers \(a,b\) are numerical weights. This is linearity in the tangent vector at one point, not a claim that temperature is a linear function throughout the patch.
\explanation{first-order}{Why is linearity at one point enough?}{A differential retains a smooth function's first-order change at that point. Higher-order terms can matter over a finite journey without changing this local linear readout. Different points generally have different differentials.}}
For any smooth scalar field \(f\), the same construction gives \(df_p(v)\coloneqq v[f]\). It does not assert that every covector field over a region is the differential of one scalar field. A temperature field changing with time would also contribute a change at a fixed ground point; that case is outside this example.
statement: The temperature differential turns a tangent velocity into an instantaneous temperature rate.

title: The readout on a board's grid
body:
To calculate the temperature readout, choose local coordinates \(x^1,x^2\). The probe visits the same ground points regardless of their labels.
Write \(\partial_i\coloneqq\partial/\partial x^i|_p\) for the coordinate basis vectors. Here \(i,j\) range over 1 and 2; a repeated upper/lower index is summed. Their dual covectors \(dx^i\) are defined by
\[\begin{aligned}
dx^i(\partial_j)&\coloneqq\delta^i{}_j,\\
dx^i(v)&=v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
Each basis covector therefore reads one coordinate component of the vector. At \(p\),
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p&=(\partial_iT)_p\,dx^i,\\
v&=v^i\partial_i,\\
dT_p(v)&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The last expression is the familiar chain-rule temperature rate \(dT(\gamma(t))/dt\), evaluated at the point being crossed.
\explanation{algebra}{Where does the component sum come from?}{Apply the covector to the vector, using linearity and the dual-basis rule:
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(\partial_iT)_p\,dx^i(v^j\partial_j)\\
&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^j\delta^i{}_j\\
&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The Kronecker delta selects matching components. No dot product or metric has entered the calculation.}
More generally, \(\omega=\omega_i dx^i\) is the coordinate expansion of a covector. The matching dual-basis normalisation is dimensionless; that does not make every physical pairing dimensionless.
statement: The dual basis reads vector components: \(dx^i(v)=v^i\), giving \(\omega(v)=\omega_i v^i\).

title: A measurement scientists can compare
body:
Suppose the local temperature derivatives are \(\partial_1T=2\,\mathrm{K/m}\) and \(\partial_2T=-1\,\mathrm{K/m}\). The probe has coordinate rates \(v^1=0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(v^2=0.2\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Its instantaneous temperature rate is
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(2)(0.5)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&\quad{}-(1)(0.2)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&=0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}.
\end{aligned}\]
The probe is warming, even though one contribution is cooling. These are coordinate rates: on an arbitrarily scaled or oblique grid, their Euclidean component length is not automatically the probe's measured physical speed.
\explanation{centimetres}{Why does a centimetre grid give the same answer?}{Relabel both coordinates from metres to centimetres. The numerical coordinate labels become 100 times larger. The probe's rates become \(50\) and \(20\,\mathrm{cm/s}\), while the temperature derivatives become \(0.02\) and \(-0.01\,\mathrm{K/cm}\). Hence
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(0.02)(50)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&\quad{}-(0.01)(20)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&=0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}.
\end{aligned}\]
These changes compensate because both calculations describe the same motion through the same temperature field. Coordinate independence does not mean dimensionlessness: the answer still has units K/s. The instantaneous rate is exact; using it over a finite journey assumes it stays constant, or gives an approximation.}
Think of \(dT_p\) as a readout attached to this point: give it a tangent velocity and it returns that velocity's temperature rate. It acts on arrows; it need not itself be drawn as an arrow.
No metric was needed for the pairing. Asking for the direction of greatest temperature increase at a fixed physical speed would require a metric to define that speed.
The same rule applies to grass growth: \(dT_p(G_p)\) is positive towards warmer ground, negative towards colder ground, and zero along an isotherm to first order.
statement: The probe warms at \(0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}\), regardless of the coordinate units.

title: The dual space of tangent vectors
body: A covector or one-form \(\omega\in T_p^*M\) is a linear map on the \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space}, written \(\omega:T_pM\rightarrow\mathbb R\). Thus \(\omega(av+bw)=a\omega(v)+b\omega(w)\). The number \(\omega(v)\), also written \(\omega_\mu v^\mu\), is the natural pairing between a covector and a vector and needs no metric.
statement: The cotangent space is the dual \(T_p^*M=\mathrm{Hom}(T_pM,\mathbb R)\) of the tangent space.

title: Covectors as linear readouts
body: Think of a covector as a linear measuring instruction attached at \(p\). It can ask how much a direction points across a family of level surfaces, how quickly a scalar reading changes along that direction, or what one coordinate component of the direction is. Different tangent vectors can give the same reading, and all vectors in the covector's kernel give zero.
statement: A covector measures a direction linearly; many different directions can give the same result.

title: A scalar need not be dimensionless
body:
A covector's pairing with a tangent vector is coordinate-independent, but its physical units depend on what is being paired. For the temperature field, \(\partial T/\partial x\) has units of kelvin per coordinate unit. Pairing \(dT\) with a small displacement gives a first-order temperature change in kelvin. Pairing it with the probe velocity gives a temperature-change rate in kelvin per second.

No metric enters either pairing. The cancellation is of coordinate dependence, not necessarily of every physical unit. A dimensionless phase change is a different example: a phase differential paired with a displacement can be dimensionless.
statement: Coordinate-independent scalar readouts can still carry physical units.

title: The same temperature change on two grids
body:
At a terrain point suppose \(\partial T/\partial x=2\,\mathrm{K/m}\). Keep \(y\) fixed and consider \(\delta x=0.5\,\mathrm m\) within the local linear approximation. The differential predicts \[dT_p(\delta x\,\partial_x)=(2\,\mathrm{K/m})(0.5\,\mathrm m)=1\,\mathrm K.\] On a centimetre-labelled grid the same calculation is \((0.02\,\mathrm{K/cm})(50\,\mathrm{cm})=1\,\mathrm K\). The covector component's numerical value decreases by 100 while the displacement component's increases by 100.

The differential gives an exact linear readout at \(p\); identifying it with the actual finite temperature difference is a first-order approximation. If temperature varies nonlinearly over the displacement, the approximation needs refinement.
statement: Metre and centimetre components predict the same first-order temperature change.

title: A directional-change calculation
body: Use dimensionless coordinates and a dimensionless scalar for this algebraic example. Let \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\). At \(p=(2,1)\), \(df=4\,dx+3\,dy\). For a tangent vector with components \(v=(1,-2)\), the change along that direction is \(df(v)=4(1)+3(-2)=-2\). The covector turns the direction into one scalar rate.
statement: For \(f=x^2+3y\) at \((2,1)\), the direction \((1,-2)\) gives \(df(v)=-2\).

title: Contours and zero change
body: On a contour map, a tangent direction along a contour produces no first-order change in height, so the height differential evaluates to zero on it. A direction crossing several contours produces a nonzero reading. Calling the differential a perpendicular arrow uses a metric to convert it to a vector; the covector itself is the rule assigning these rates.
statement: A scalar differential vanishes on directions tangent to its level curves.

title: Why covectors appear in physics
body: A wave phase \(\phi\) has covector \(d\phi\), which measures phase change along any spacetime direction. In mechanics a momentum one-form pairs with an infinitesimal displacement or velocity to make a scalar contribution to work or action. These pairings explain why lower-index objects arise naturally rather than merely as vectors with altered notation.
statement: Phase differentials and momentum one-forms turn directions into scalar readouts.

title: Do not assume the metric too soon
body: Tangent vectors and covectors are distinct before a metric is chosen. A nondegenerate metric supplies an additional map between them, written as lowering or raising an index. Familiar Euclidean pictures quietly use this map when they draw a gradient covector as an ordinary perpendicular arrow; the cotangent space itself does not depend on it.
statement: A metric can identify vectors with covectors, but the dual space exists without one.

title: Tensors varying over spacetime
body: GR describes spacetime geometry and matter using quantities attached to every event. Scalars, vectors and covectors are the first examples; tensors extend their coordinate-independent meaning to quantities with several inputs or indices. Begin with what a tensor does at one point, then let that object vary smoothly from point to point.
statement: A tensor field gives a coordinate-independent geometric object at every point.

title: A smooth field of multilinear objects
body:
Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. At a point \(p\), a tensor of type \((r,s)\) is a real-valued multilinear map with \(r\) cotangent-vector inputs and \(s\) tangent-vector inputs. Multilinear means linear in each input when the others are held fixed.
A tensor field assigns one tensor of the same type smoothly to every point of a region. In a smooth local basis its component functions are smooth. Components depend on the basis; the tensor they describe does not.
A scalar field has type \((0,0)\). A vector is a type-\((1,0)\) tensor acting on a covector by the natural pairing. A covector is a type-\((0,1)\) tensor acting on a vector.
\explanation{point}{Must the input vectors be at the same point?}{Yes. A tensor at \(p\) acts on tangent vectors in \(T_pM\) and covectors in \(T_p^*M\). Comparing or transporting inputs from different points requires additional structure; a tensor field alone supplies no such rule.}
statement: A tensor field assigns a fixed-type tensor smoothly to each point of a manifold.

title: Point-by-point objects
body:
At a terrain point \(p\), the temperature \(T(p)\), grass-growth vector \(G_p\) and differential \(dT_p\) are different kinds of object. A smooth field supplies the appropriate object at every point. In a smooth local basis its component functions vary smoothly.
A tensor contraction is performed at one point. For example, pairing \(dT_p\) with \(G_p\) produces a scalar there. Repeating the pairing throughout a region produces a scalar field.
\explanation{contraction}{Calculate one pointwise pairing}{Suppose \(\omega_i=(2,-1)\) and \(V^i=(3,4)\) in a two-dimensional basis. The natural pairing is
\[\omega_i V^i=2(3)+(-1)(4)=2.\]
These numbers are dimensionless in this algebraic example. The matching upper/lower index is summed. Physical pairings can carry units, and this pairing needs no metric.}
Vectors at different points belong to different tangent spaces. A field does not by itself give a rule for comparing or transporting them.
statement: Fields supply local objects; contractions combine them at the same point.

title: Scalars, vectors, and higher tensors
body:
In the terrain survey, temperature is an order-zero scalar field, grass growth an order-one vector field, and the temperature differential an order-one covector field.
For GR, the metric \(g_{\mu
u}\) and covariant stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu
u}\) have type \((0,2)\). The Riemann curvature tensor in the form \(R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}\) has type \((1,3)\) and total order four. Its many components describe one geometric object, not many unrelated scalar fields.
A metric can raise or lower indices, producing related tensors of different type. For example \(T^{\mu
u}\) is a raised form of \(T_{\mu
u}\); raising is additional metric-dependent structure, not a change of coordinate labels.
statement: Scalars, vectors, covectors, metrics and curvature tensors are different tensor types.

title: Not just an array of components
body:
A component array describes a tensor only together with its basis and transformation behaviour. Two charts can assign different arrays to the same field if those arrays obey the tensor transformation law throughout their overlap. Equal array sizes or constant entries do not establish that relation.
The \cref{tensor transformation law}{math.tensor_transformation_law} makes this precise. Not every array of quantities with index labels transforms tensorially; the connection coefficients used later in GR are an important warning.
statement: An array represents a tensor only with a basis and the correct transformation behaviour.

title: Indices as bookkeeping
body: Indices let us calculate with components without writing out every sum. The practical skills are to recognise upper and lower indices, distinguish a summed label from an unsummed one, and check that an equation has the same free indices on both sides. Abstract-index notation is a useful later refinement, not a prerequisite for these calculations.
statement: Indices record component slots, sums and the shape of tensor equations.

title: Component labels and abstract slots
body:
In a chosen coordinate basis for a \cref{tensor field}{math.tensor_field}, \(V^i\) lists a vector's components and \(\omega_i\) lists a covector's components. The superscript is an index, not a power: \(V^2\) means the second component here, whereas \((V^1)^2\) squares the first component.
An expression such as \(A^i{}_{j}\) has two index slots. Fixing both labels selects one entry of its component matrix.
\explanation{abstract}{What changes in abstract-index notation?}{Abstract indices such as \(a,b\) describe the tensor's slots and contractions without choosing a numerical basis. Thus \(A^a{}_{b}\) describes a type-\((1,1)\) tensor. Component indices describe entries after a basis is chosen. Either notation can have free or dummy indices; the distinction is not curved versus flat space.}
The calculations on this page use component indices unless explicitly stated otherwise.
statement: Component indices label basis entries; abstract indices describe tensor slots without choosing a basis.

title: Component indices
statement: An index range records dimension; index number and position record tensor type.

title: Repeated and free indices
statement: Repeated upper/lower indices are summed; free indices must match on both sides.

title: Indexed need not mean coordinate-bound
body:
Using components does not make an equation coordinate-dependent in meaning. A correctly formed tensor equation remains true after a smooth change of chart. Conversely, matching free indices is necessary but does not prove that the objects in an equation are tensors.
\explanation{raising}{Can an index simply be moved up or down?}{No. A metric is needed to lower a vector index:
\[V_\mu=g_{\mu\nu}V^\nu.\]
The free index \(\mu\) remains on both sides; \(\nu\) is summed. The inverse metric raises indices. Neither operation is the same as renaming a dummy index.}
statement: Matching indices is necessary for a tensor equation, but does not establish tensorial behaviour.

title: Components that transform correctly
body:
In the terrain survey, two boards can give different component tables for the same measurement. This is expected: a component says how an object is expressed in a particular basis. Changing the basis must change the components in compensation.
For a vector, follow the same route in both coordinate grids and use the chain rule. For a covector, require its linear readout of that vector to stay the same. These two requirements give opposite transformation factors.
A tensor with several slots is linear in each slot separately, so it receives one factor for each index. This is a consistency rule for descriptions, not a law that evolves the physical field or a claim that its components are constant.
statement: Different component arrays can describe the same tensor in different coordinate bases.

title: One Jacobian factor for every index
body:
Consider overlapping coordinates \(x^i\) and \(y^a\). The \cref{coordinate transition}{math.coordinate_transformation} gives an invertible Jacobian and its inverse:
\[\begin{aligned}
J^a{}_i&\coloneqq\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i},\\
K^i{}_a&\coloneqq\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}.
\end{aligned}\]
At the same manifold point, tensor components in the \(y\) basis receive one \(J\) factor for each upper index and one \(K\) factor for each lower index. Old component indices are summed; new ones are free.
For example, a type-\((1,1)\) tensor obeys
\[T_y^a{}_b=J^a{}_i K^j{}_b T_x^i{}_j.\]
Here subscripts \(x,y\) identify the coordinate description, not extra tensor indices. For nonlinear transitions the factors depend on the point. This is a passive change of description of the same tensor.
statement: Every upper index receives a forward Jacobian; every lower index receives its inverse.

title: Vector and covector cases
body:
Let \(x^i\) and \(y^a\) be overlapping coordinates, with all quantities evaluated at the same point \(p\). A vector \(V\) can be represented by a curve through \(p\). Applying the chain rule gives
\[V_y^a=\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}V_x^i.\]
A covector \(\omega\) must give the same scalar readout on that vector in either chart. Its components therefore obey
\[\omega^y_a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\omega^x_i.\]
The superscripts \(x,y\) on \(\omega\) name the chart, not extra indices. Each repeated upper/lower index is summed. Understanding that convention is the role of \cref{index notation}{math.index_notation}.
The forward and inverse factors cancel in \(\omega^y_a V_y^a=\omega^x_i V_x^i\). No metric is needed: this is the natural vector/covector pairing, not an orthogonal dot-product assumption.
\explanation{why-inverse}{Derive the covector rule from the pairing}{The scalar readout must agree for every vector:
\[\omega^y_a V_y^a=\omega^x_i V_x^i.\]
Substitute the vector rule. Since this must hold for every \(V_x^i\),
\[\omega^y_a\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}=\omega^x_i.\]
Multiplying by the inverse Jacobian gives the displayed covector transformation. No metric entered the argument.}
statement: Vectors and covectors transform oppositely, preserving their scalar pairing.

title: One factor per index
body:
A \cref{tensor}{math.tensor_field} is multilinear in its tangent/cotangent inputs. This forces one transformation factor per component index.
At a point use overlapping coordinates \(x^i,y^a\). Write \(J^a{}_i=\partial y^a/\partial x^i\) and \(K^i{}_a=\partial x^i/\partial y^a\). The basis covectors and vectors obey
\[\begin{aligned}
dy^a&=J^a{}_i\,dx^i,\\
\partial/\partial y^b&=K^j{}_b\,\partial/\partial x^j.
\end{aligned}\]
A type-\((1,2)\) tensor accepts one covector and two vectors. Its new components are its readouts on these new basis inputs. Substituting the three basis changes and using multilinearity gives
\[T_y^a{}_{bc}
 =J^a{}_i K^j{}_b K^k{}_c T_x^i{}_{jk}.\]
The old indices \(i,j,k\) are summed. The new indices \(a,b,c\) are free. Repeating the same argument for any number of slots gives the general rule.
For a covariant order-two tensor such as a metric, there are just two inverse factors:
\[g^y_{ab}=K^i{}_a K^j{}_b g^x_{ij}.\]
\explanation{factors}{Why can the factors be pulled outside?}{Linearity in a single slot allows its basis-change coefficients to be pulled out while the other inputs are fixed. Apply that step once to each slot. Multiplying these independent coefficients gives the product of Jacobian factors; it is not an assumption that the original component functions are linear in position.}
statement: Multilinearity supplies one transformation factor for each tensor index.

title: Not unchanged components
body:
Tensorial does not mean that every component remains numerically unchanged. It means the components transform by the rule appropriate to their index slots, so the underlying geometric object and its scalar measurements are unchanged at the same point.
\explanation{cancel}{See the Jacobians cancel in a contraction}{Use \(V_y^a=J^a{}_j V_x^j\), \(\omega^y_a=K^i{}_a\omega^x_i\), and \(K^i{}_aJ^a{}_j=\delta^i{}_j\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\omega^y_a V_y^a&=\omega^x_i K^i{}_aJ^a{}_j V_x^j\\
&=\omega^x_i\delta^i{}_j V_x^j\\
&=\omega^x_j V_x^j.
\end{aligned}\]
This is pointwise coordinate independence, not a claim that the scalar has the same value at different manifold points.}
Ordinary partial derivatives of tensor components generally introduce extra terms under nonlinear chart changes. GR uses a covariant derivative to correct for this; its construction is beyond this module.
statement: Coordinate independence does not mean that tensor components stay fixed.

title: Type, order and rank
statement: Tensor type \((r,s)\) counts upper and lower slots; total order is \(r+s\).

title: What a tensor measures
body:
A covector accepts one vector and returns a scalar. A covariant order-two tensor \(B\), of type \((0,2)\), accepts two vectors and returns a scalar:
\[B(V,W)=B_{ij}V^iW^j.\]
It is linear in each vector separately. Holding \(W\) fixed makes \(B(V,W)\) a linear readout of \(V\); holding \(V\) fixed makes it a linear readout of \(W\).
\explanation{multilinear}{Why separately linear, not jointly linear?}{For fixed \(W\),
\[B(aV+bU,W)=aB(V,W)+bB(U,W).\]
But scaling both inputs multiplies the result twice: \(B(2V,2W)=4B(V,W)\). This is bilinearity, not linearity in the pair treated as a single input.}
More generally a tensor of type \((r,s)\), viewed as a scalar-valued multilinear map, accepts \(r\) covectors and \(s\) vectors. The upper indices are the slots paired with covectors; the lower indices pair with vectors.
\explanation{vector-slot}{How can a vector be a tensor in this description?}{A vector \(V\) acts on a covector by returning \(\omega(V)\). Thus a type-\((1,0)\) tensor accepts one covector. A covector, of type \((0,1)\), accepts one vector. Neither identification requires a metric.}
statement: A tensor accepts vectors and covectors, returning a scalar linearly in each input separately.

title: A metric gives a two-input measurement
body:
At one point of a two-dimensional surface, a metric \(g\) is a symmetric bilinear map pairing two tangent vectors. In a local basis suppose
\[g_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]
Use dimensionless component values for this algebraic example. For \(V^i=(1,2)\),
\[\begin{aligned}
g(V,V)&=4(1)^2+1(2)^2\\
&=8.
\end{aligned}\]
The answer is not \(1^2+2^2=5\): these coordinates are not a unit orthonormal grid. For a displacement with physical units, the metric pairing supplies squared length with the corresponding units.
For spacetime a Lorentzian metric supplies an interval rather than a positive squared length for every vector. The two-input tensor structure remains the same.
statement: For \(g_{ij}=\mathrm{diag}(4,1)\) and \(V^i=(1,2)\), the metric pairing gives \(g(V,V)=8\).

title: One grid stretched by a factor of two
body:
Use numerical coordinate labels with \(x'=2x\). At one point let \(V^x=3\) and \(\omega_x=8\). Then
\[\begin{aligned}
V^{x'}&=2(3)=6,\\
\omega_{x'}&=\tfrac12(8)=4.
\end{aligned}\]
The pairing is \(8(3)=24\) before relabelling and \(4(6)=24\) afterwards. The component values change while the readout stays fixed.
\explanation{two-index}{What happens to a two-index tensor?}{If the same rescaling is applied to a one-dimensional coordinate, a covariant component \(B_{xx}\) receives two inverse factors:
\[B_{x'x'}=\tfrac14 B_{xx}.\]
A mixed component \(A^x{}_{x}\) receives one factor of two and one of a half, so it stays unchanged in this particular rescaling. This does not make every mixed component invariant under general changes of basis.}
statement: Rescaling coordinate labels changes components while preserving the scalar pairing.

title: Specifying a smooth structure
body:
Start with a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space \(M\) that is locally homeomorphic to \(\mathbb R^n\). Choose local homeomorphisms \(x_\alpha:U_\alpha\to x_\alpha(U_\alpha)\) whose regions cover \(M\).
Require every overlap conversion \(x_\beta\circ x_\alpha^{-1}\), and its inverse, to be smooth. Enlarge the compatible collection to its maximal smooth atlas; that atlas specifies the smooth structure.
This is a construction/definition of the setting, not a proof that an arbitrary space is a manifold. No distance or curvature has yet been assigned.
\explanation{compatibility}{What does an overlap condition buy?}{A scalar function is smooth when its expressions in the charts are smooth. If overlap conversions are smooth, replacing one chart by a compatible neighbour preserves this property by composition. Calculus therefore does not depend on which member of the atlas supplies the labels.}
statement: Compatible local charts specify smooth structure; this is starting data, not a curvature result.

title: Constructing a chart on a surface
body:
Suppose \(M\) is already a smooth two-dimensional surface. Choose a smooth projection \(\pi:M\to B\) onto a flat board \(B\), and straight board coordinates \(\ell:B\to\mathbb R^2\). At a point \(p\) where the derivative of \(\ell\circ\pi\) is invertible, the inverse-function theorem gives a small neighbourhood \(U\) on which
\[x\coloneqq(\ell\circ\pi)|_U\]
has a smooth inverse. This restriction is a coordinate chart.
The theorem guarantees a local patch, not a global map or preservation of lengths. If the projection overlaps itself or its derivative becomes singular, shrink the patch or choose another board.
\explanation{board}{Why does a tangent board work nearby?}{For a regular embedded surface, projection onto its tangent plane has an invertible derivative at the point of tangency. An invertible choice of scale and straight axes on that plane preserves this property. Away from that point, the chart's coordinate basis belongs to the ground surface, not to the physical board.}
statement: A smooth surface projection is a chart locally when its derivative is nonsingular.

title: From a history to a curve
body:
Take a spacetime manifold \(M\) and an interval \(I\) of real numbers. Associate each parameter value \(\lambda\in I\) with the event occupied by the particle, writing this map as \(\gamma(\lambda)\). Require its coordinate expressions to vary smoothly wherever a chart covers the history.
On an overlap, composing with the chart transition gives another description of the same map, so the curve is not tied to one coordinate system. A smooth strictly increasing reparametrisation changes the labels along the same oriented history.
This construction represents a proposed history. It does not derive its dynamics or decide whether it is timelike or null; a metric and physical laws supply those further restrictions.
statement: An ordered smooth history defines a map from a parameter interval into spacetime.

title: Building tensors from vectors and covectors
body:
Fix a point \(p\) and its finite-dimensional \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space} \(T_pM\) with dual \cref{cotangent space}{math.cotangent_space} \(T_p^*M\). For vectors \(V,W\in T_pM\) and covectors \(\alpha,\beta\in T_p^*M\), define
\[(\alpha\otimes\beta)(V,W)\coloneqq\alpha(V)\beta(W).\]
Linearity of each covector makes this a bilinear map of two vector inputs. Sums of such products remain bilinear.
Choose a basis \(e_i\) and its dual \(\varepsilon^i\), with \(\varepsilon^i(e_j)=\delta^i{}_j\). Every bilinear scalar-valued map \(B\) has the expansion
\[B=B_{ij}\,\varepsilon^i\otimes\varepsilon^j,\]
where \(B_{ij}=B(e_i,e_j)\), with repeated indices summed.
For a mixed tensor, include vector factors as well: a vector acts on a covector by \(\omega\mapsto\omega(V)\). Taking products and linear combinations gives arbitrary finite-dimensional type-\((r,s)\) tensors. Letting their coefficients vary smoothly in local smooth bases gives a tensor field.
This constructs the tensor space; it does not determine the coefficients of a physical field. Geometry or physical laws must supply those.
\explanation{basis}{Why does the bilinear expansion recover the map?}{Expand \(V=V^ie_i\) and \(W=W^je_j\). Bilinearity gives \(B(V,W)=B(e_i,e_j)V^iW^j\). The dual basis reads \(V^i\) and \(W^j\), so the displayed tensor product has exactly the same value on every pair of inputs.}
statement: Products of vector/covector pairings and their linear combinations construct tensors at one point.

title: Why the scalar pairing becomes a sum
body:
At one point choose tangent basis \(e_i\) and dual covector basis \(\varepsilon^j\), so \(\varepsilon^j(e_i)=\delta^j{}_i\). Write a vector and covector as
\[V=V^ie_i,\qquad\omega=\omega_j\varepsilon^j.\]
Linearity then gives
\[\begin{aligned}
\omega(V)&=\omega_j V^i\,\varepsilon^j(e_i)\\
 &=\omega_j V^i\,\delta^j{}_i\\
 &=\omega_i V^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The repeated upper/lower label is an instruction to sum matching slots. The name of that dummy label is irrelevant: replacing both copies of \(i\) by \(k\) changes no term.
This motivates Einstein summation notation; the notation itself is a convention. More general contractions pair one vector-like and one covector-like slot of a tensor, reducing its total order by two.
No metric is required for this natural pairing. Raising an index first would be a separate, metric-dependent operation.
statement: Expanding in dual bases turns a coordinate-independent pairing into an upper/lower contraction.

title: A locally chartable surface
body: The point \(p\) lies in a small neighbourhood of a smooth surface \(M\). The curved grid is a picture of local labels, not a measurement of lengths. No surrounding embedding space is required by the abstract manifold definition.
statement: A curved surface can have ordinary local coordinates without a global flat grid.

title: From ground points to labels
body: The left patch \(U\) and the right coordinate image describe the same points. The map labelled \(\phi\) is a chart; its inverse locates the ground point from its labels. The flat rectangle is a space of coordinate numbers, not evidence that the ground is physically flat.
statement: A chart and its inverse connect one local region with its coordinate image.

title: One point in two coordinate grids
body: The red point appears in both charts. The connecting cue identifies its two coordinate records; it is not a trajectory or displacement. The transition acts on labels on an overlap, and its derivative controls the change of vector components there.
statement: Coordinate transitions connect two descriptions of the same point.

title: A history drawn in coordinates
body: The horizontal axis is one spatial coordinate and the vertical axis is \(ct\), with \(c\) the speed of light. The blue curve passes through successive events. Another chart can change the curve drawn on the page without changing the physical history. This is a spacetime plot, not a single-time spatial track.
statement: The event dots belong to one spacetime history, shown in a particular coordinate plot.

title: Linear readouts of tangent directions
body: The level-line motif suggests directions that give the same readout and directions that cross the levels. It is a mnemonic for a linear rule on tangent vectors. Any gradient-like arrow in this picture uses an auxiliary geometric drawing; a covector need not be identified with a vector or depend on a metric.
statement: A covector assigns scalar readings to tangent vectors at one point.

title: A tensor at every point
body: The repeated \(T\) glyphs indicate assignments at different manifold points. Each tensor acts on inputs at its own point, and its components are taken in a basis there. Smoothness links the local descriptions; the diagram does not supply a transport rule between tangent spaces.
statement: A field supplies local tensors throughout a region, rather than one isolated component array.

title: One tensor and its component array
body: The abstract symbol and the small array represent the same kind of geometric object at one point. Numerical component labels choose entries after a basis is fixed. Abstract indices instead describe tensor slots and contractions; neither notation changes the object or its tensor type.
statement: A chosen basis turns an abstract tensor into a component description.

title: Changing the component description
body: The arrow labelled \(\Lambda\) summarises a component transformation; it does not deform the tensor physically. For general overlapping charts the individual factors are Jacobians or inverse Jacobians at the point, and need not be constant. The precise factor for each index is stated in the transformation rule.
statement: Different component arrays can represent the same tensor after a change of coordinates.
